scenario: Today's systems track is about avoiding repeated computation. LEAP reads how long a request will generate straight from the serving model's prefill hidden states and uses it to order requests. HiState and Flide deal with the recomputation caused by recurrent-layer states that cannot be cut back in hybrid models, and ACCT lets one model reuse the KV cache another model of the same family has already computed. ARK keeps KV cache transfers in disaggregated serving from colliding on the same link. On hardware, a B200 versus B300 benchmark shows the newer card is not faster everywhere, and MemX searches parallel configurations for training on mixed-vendor GPU clusters.

papers.title: LEAP: Efficient LLM Inference Scheduling with Generalizable Length Prediction
papers.authors: Kwan Yan, Jialun Zhong, Yanzeng Li
papers.abstract: Length-aware scheduling reduces request latency in LLM serving by prioritizing shorter requests. However, despite their large model sizes, length predictors can suffer degraded ranking performance under domain and task shifts, and adapting them can require costly retraining. Their prediction overhead can further offset the benefits of scheduling. To improve the generalization and efficiency of length-aware scheduling, we propose \textbf{LEAP}, a length prediction system with fast online adaptation and asynchronous CPU execution. LEAP reuses the serving model's prefill hidden states, which contain information about the output length, and extracts this signal through a linear readout. To adapt to substantial domain and task shifts, it updates the readout at test time through recursive least squares, using completed requests as supervision without gradient computation or historical-data replay. Prediction and updates run asynchronously on CPU, while prediction and initial batch ordering overlap the remaining GPU prefill. Across the evaluated cross-domain transfers, LEAP retains strong ranking performance, and online adaptation improves Spearman correlation by 64.7\% under a larger domain shift. Serving experiments show that LEAP reduces average per-token latency by 15.9--40.8\% compared with the evaluated length predictors, while achieving 1.9\% higher throughput with $30{,}569\times$ fewer predictor parameters than the strongest evaluated baseline.
papers.summary: Running short requests first clearly lowers average latency, but only if you know roughly how long each request will generate, and existing length predictors rank worse when the domain changes while costing GPU time of their own. LEAP finds that the hidden states the serving model computes during prefill already carry an output-length signal, and a single linear layer on one layer's hidden state can read it out, with no separate encoder. The linear layer runs on CPU, in parallel with the rest of prefill on the GPU, so it takes no GPU time. After each request finishes, LEAP uses recursive least squares to correct the layer's weights from that request's true length with a closed-form update, with no gradients and no replay of old data. In single-GPU experiments on ShareGPT traffic, average per-token latency is 15.9% to 40.8% lower than with several existing predictors. ==A length predictor should be judged by latency after scheduling and by its own cost.==

papers.title: HiState: Hierarchical Prefix Cache Management for Hybrid LLM Serving in Agentic Workloads
papers.authors: Zaifeng Pan, Lucas Wang, Xinwei Qiang, Yanbo Zhou, Chang Chen, Zhengding Hu, Yue Guan, Yufei Ding
papers.abstract: Hybrid large language models combine full-attention and recurrent linear layers to reduce inference costs. Prefix caching can further reduce redundant computation across requests, but a recurrent checkpoint cannot recover an earlier state corresponding to a shorter prefix. Existing hybrid prefix caching systems retain checkpoints at selected boundaries to support common reuse patterns in conventional conversations. However, agent workloads modify and revisit earlier contexts, exposing reusable prefixes whose checkpoints were never saved or have already been evicted. A straightforward approach is to retain more checkpoints to reduce recomputation, but their cumulative footprint can displace reusable prefixes from other sessions and cause additional cache misses. To address these problems, we present HiState, a prefix cache management system for hybrid models serving agent workloads. Our key observation is that prefix reuse accesses all matching key-value (KV) entries but only one recurrent checkpoint, regardless of how many checkpoints are retained. This asymmetry allows HiState to retain historical checkpoints on SSD while prioritizing fast memory for KV entries: each hit retrieves only one checkpoint whose size is independent of context length. Within this hierarchy, we propose adaptive interval control to balance checkpoint storage against recomputation, and unified eviction to coordinate checkpoint sparsification with reclamation of stale trajectories. We implement HiState on top of vLLM and evaluate it on two public coding-agent trace datasets and controlled microbenchmarks. On real agent traces, HiState achieves up to 5.73x and 5.44x speedups in p99 TTFT over vLLM-Marconi and SGLang-HiCache, respectively.
papers.summary: The recurrent layers of a hybrid model compress the whole prefix into a fixed-size snapshot, and it cannot be cut back to an earlier position. So even when the KV is still cached, if the snapshot at the match point was never saved or has already been evicted, a long stretch must be recomputed from an earlier snapshot, or from scratch. HiState exploits an asymmetry: a cache hit reads every matching KV entry but only one snapshot, and the snapshot's size does not depend on context length. So it keeps many historical snapshots on SSD and saves fast memory for KV, and it puts snapshots and KV into one eviction queue. Each item's score is its last access time plus the extra tokens to recompute if it is removed, divided by the space it frees; the lowest score goes first. On two public coding-agent traces, it reaches p99 TTFT speedups of up to 5.73 times over Marconi on vLLM. ==Extra snapshots cost no fast memory, and each hit reads only one from slow storage.==

deep_reading.title: HiState: Hierarchical Prefix Cache Management for Hybrid LLM Serving in Agentic Workloads

papers.title: MemX: Memory-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous GPU Training
papers.authors: Lin Meng, Yuzhong Sun, Jie Zhu
papers.abstract: Cross-vendor heterogeneous GPU clusters are increasingly used for large-scale model training. However, their GPUs differ substantially in compute power, memory capacity, and interconnect characteristics. Existing automatic parallelism training systems usually minimize iteration time while treating memory as a hard constraint, almost failing in resolving the compute--memory asymmetry of cross-vendor clusters regardless correlation between memory and throughput. In this paper, we present MemX, a new memory-aware automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes iteration time, peak memory usage, and cross-GPU memory balance. MemX consists of a weighted-product objective function, heterogeneous recomputation strategies, a minimal-set profiler, interpolation-based data augmentation, a dual-output XGBoost predictor, and a hash-signature prediction cache, in order to accelerate search of large-scale auto-parallel best configurations at lower cost. We implement MemX on Megatron-LM and evaluate it against four automatic parallelism baselines on two heterogeneous clusters. MemX achieves the lowest prediction Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 12.17% and is the only method that identifies the real Top-1 configuration under both time-based and memory-balance rankings. In terms of search cost and search space, MemX searches 31,240 configurations in 26.5 seconds, while an end-to-end profiling baseline is extrapolated to require about 17 days at the same scale. The simulation study that extends the measured 20-GPU data to 40-GPU and 60-GPU clusters further illustrates the effectiveness of MemX at larger scales.
papers.summary: When a large model is trained on a cluster that mixes GPUs from several vendors, MemX makes memory balance across GPUs an explicit search objective, and it lets small-memory GPUs recompute more while large-memory GPUs recompute nothing. That way it finds parallel configurations that neither run out of memory nor leave memory badly uneven across GPUs. For every candidate it estimates iteration time, peak memory, and the variance of memory use across GPUs, combines the three with weights into one score, and the lowest score wins. On a three-vendor cluster, under both a time-based ranking and a memory-balance ranking, it is the only method that puts the real best configuration first; in online search it covers 31,240 configurations in 26.5 seconds. What it buys is memory headroom, not speed: in the real deployment, its pick is 9.3% slower than the fastest configuration. ==On a mixed cluster memory and compute are out of proportion, so the search objective must include memory.==

deep_reading.title: MemX: Memory-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous GPU Training

papers.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
papers.authors: Mohsen Zand, Trung Dac Nguyen, H. Birali Runesha
papers.abstract: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO. We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.
papers.summary: The B300 is the upgrade to the B200, with more memory, but it is not faster on every task. The University of Chicago's Research Computing Center measured both on two eight-GPU clusters, and on convolutional network inference the B200 was up to 5.6 times faster than the B300. Per-GPU power shows why: on those tasks the B300 drew only 36% to 53% of its power limit, and the time went to the cost of each individual kernel; on ViT-Large, where the B300 wins, both cards ran close to full power. Separately, on two B300 nodes with identical chips, time to first token was 2.1 times higher on one, only because they ran different vLLM builds. ==Before buying a new card, measure it on your own workloads and your own software versions.==

papers.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
papers.authors: Bobo Li, Jiajia Song, Hao Fei, Wynne Hsu, Mong Li Lee
papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
papers.summary: Inference engines built for generation handle the decision models used in agent systems badly. These models do not generate long text: they attach many short questions to one shared context, and each question outputs a single category. Existing engines either recompute the shared context for every question, or pack the questions together so they interfere and the output probabilities drift. Flide packs the shared context and all questions into one token sequence computed in a single pass. Indices kept on the GPU record which shared context each question belongs to. Attention layers use them so a question sees only the shared context and itself, and recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet restart every question from the state at the end of the shared context. The result matches a separate computation exactly, and queries are answered up to 9.5 times faster than with vLLM and SGLang.

papers.title: Trainable Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.authors: Anastasiia Prutianova, Alina Bogdanova, Mikhail Shutov, Dmitrii Poimanov, Anatoly Gorkov, Ilia Zharikov
papers.abstract: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.
papers.summary: Vector quantization can compress an LLM to about 2 bits per weight, but the harder it compresses, the more quality it loses. It splits weights into small groups and replaces each group with the closest vector in a codebook, a shared table of representative vectors. Picking the vector is a discrete choice that gradients cannot fix directly, so existing methods only make each layer's quantized output match the original, one layer at a time. TVQ keeps trainable continuous weights behind the quantized ones: in the forward pass each group of continuous weights looks up its closest codebook vector and computes with it, and the backward pass sends the gradient straight to the continuous weights. The lookup is redone after every update, so once the continuous weights move far enough, a different codebook vector is chosen. That lets the quantized model be optimized for any training objective; the paper uses block-wise knowledge distillation. LLaMA2-70B at 2 bits loses only 1% accuracy on common question-answering benchmarks.

papers.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
papers.authors: Yuzhe Liu, Haolin Tian, Tonghan Wang
papers.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
papers.summary: When models of different sizes from the same family are mixed, switching models means prefilling the same context again. ACCT lets the target model use a KV cache another model has already computed: a small model reads a long context, and a large model answers without rereading the text. A small scoring module reads the source model's hidden states and scores each context token for each attention head, trained on how much deleting that token would hurt the answer. How many tokens each head keeps is a learned parameter, the counts across heads stay within one total budget, and each head keeps its highest-scoring tokens. It then uses a trained conversion module to turn the selected tokens' representations into keys and values for the matching target layers and heads. With KV cut by 75%, the target model matches or beats its original quality; on contexts of about 19K tokens, the conversion is 6.5 to 21.2 times faster than the target's own prefill.

papers.title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
papers.authors: Jean Lucien Randrianantenaina, Hung Nguyen, Nasib Ullah, Jinbin Zhang, Nilesh Gupta, Inderjit S. Dhillon, Rohit Babbar
papers.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
papers.summary: When an LLM is pruned so that 90% of its weights are zero, one-shot pruning degrades sharply, and the strongest method, ELSA, needs optimizer state as large as the model. ETAPS tightens sparsity over several stages, pruning a little more each time, while training weight increments to make up the loss. The increments sit on a fixed, small number of positions; when one is pruned, its slot goes to a surviving weight with the largest accumulated gradient. After each stage it scores weights as the patched weight's absolute value times that position's accumulated gradient, and the next stage prunes the lowest. Across six models it beats ELSA's perplexity at every sparsity tested. Pruning LLaMA2-7B to 90% sparsity takes one H200 instead of ELSA's four.

papers.title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
papers.authors: Hung-Chun Lin, Ting-Wei Hsu, Chung-En Ho, Ahmed Saeed
papers.abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.
papers.summary: When prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, the KV cache must move from one pool to the other, and each transfer lasts hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, making it a huge flow on the network. Switches pick paths with ECMP by hashing packet headers, so two such flows that hash onto the same uplink share it for seconds while neighboring links sit idle. ARK uses the fact that these flows last long: senders tell each other in advance and choose source ports so that concurrent large flows hash onto different spine switches, with no switch changes and no reordering at the receiver. In packet-level RDMA simulation under moderate load, mean flow completion time drops by up to 27.3% and mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.

papers.title: Making Kubernetes AI-Ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin on Day One
papers.abstract: Configuring and optimizing Kubernetes for new GPU hardware such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin is complex and error-prone. Drivers, kernels, runtimes, networking,...
papers.summary: Getting a new generation of GPU racks running on Kubernetes right away is hard: if the driver, kernel, NICs or scheduling plugins are mismatched in any one place, jobs fail to start or run below capacity. This NVIDIA blog post shows how its AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) handles this for Vera Rubin NVL72. It captures validated settings for the driver, kernel, resource-allocation plugin and more as reusable recipes, generates deployment bundles, and then checks deployment, conformance and cross-node NCCL bandwidth on the running cluster. Validation on early hardware already caught an architecture-detection bug that kept crashing the resource-allocation plugin, and the fix has shipped in the official release. Teams upgrading from GB200 can use this list to plan ahead.
